newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers wage fierce battle to save dike.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers wage fierce battle to save dike.

text.p: German authorities on Wednesday began evacuating villages in the Oder River valley while more than 1,000 soldiers and relief workers waged a fevered battle to stop a collapsing dike from breaking open.

Helicopters flew in low over the trees like a scene out of a Vietnam War movie, hovering briefly to pick up nets filled with five tonnes of sand then veering off to carry their load to the dike as another approached in a seemingly endless rotation.

"We have started the evacuation because the dike has collapsed, but the German army is working hard and we hope to get things under control," said Thomas Jakob, spokesman for the crisis committee in Bad Freienwalde.
Witnesses said water was leaking so strongly from the dike that it was already filling the village of Hohenwutzen.
Brandenburg state government officials said the chances that the dike would hold were "less than 10 percent".

Some of the worst floods this century have hit Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

In the villages below the main barrier still holding back the swelling Oder River that divides Germany and Poland, sirens interrupted the afternoon stillness and families began packing up their few belongings and prepared to leave their homes, not knowing when they would return.

Earlier, villagers who had been helping to secure the dikes were sent home to pack up their belongings and bring their families in safety as a 50-metre (yard) section of the dam near the village of Altglietzen collapsed, causing panic among aid workers who thought the dike was about to rip open.
"We were all working up on the dike," said Endrik Salewsky, a 58-year-old builder, who was packing living room furniture, refrigerator, TV set and other belongings onto a flatbed truck.
"There was water leaking everywhere and then the dike sank and a big split appeared in the road. That's when they sent us all away."

Locking up a shed behind his new home in Schiffmuehle, a village with 300 residents in the path of the water should the dam break, Salewsky looked sadly up at a barrier of plastic he had wrapped around the house, covering the first floor.
"If we're lucky, the water will only rise up to here. We just moved in this Easter," he said, shaking a tear from his eye. "I guess we have to move out again."

About 900 soldiers fought overnight to support a critical section of a dike on a 70-km stretch of river along the low-lying Oderbruch region, where some 5,000 of the 19,000 inhabitants were evacuated last week.

Oderbruch, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago by Frederik the Great to create fertile farmland and is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
Farmers in the village of Altranft were hurriedly packing the last of their 2,000 heads of cattle onto transporters, but said they didn't know what would happen if the valley flooded.
"If there is a flood and all the grain is destroyed we won't have enough feed for the animals and we'll have to slaughter them," said Joern Thiele.
The Oder dikes have not failed since 1947, when floods poured into the valley when the dike burst at Reitwein, north of Frankfurt an der Oder.
There have been several breaks in the dam further south over the past two weeks and over 100 homes in the villages of Wiesenau and Ziltendorf are still underwater and thousands of people displaced.
Officials will begin inoculations this week as a preventive measure to ward off any diseases from the rotting carcasses of dead animals caught helplessly in the rushing stream.

Earlier on Wednesday, floods showed signs of receding after a fresh high-water surge expected overnight did not materialise, although officials warned that many flood-barriers were water-logged and riddled with weak spots.
The European Union proposed on Wednesday 1.5 million Ecu ($1.6 million) in relief aid for the German state of Brandenburg in order to help the battered region cope with the flooding.
